Assortment optimization under the perception-adjusted Luce model

Gerardo Berbeglia ††thanks: Melbourne Business School, The University of Melbourne, Australia. E-mail:˜g.berbeglia@mbs.edu    Mashbat Suzuki ††thanks: School of Computer Science & Engineering, UNSW Sydney, Australia. E-mail:˜mashbats@gmail.com    Matthew K. Tam ††thanks: School of Mathematics & Statistics, The University of Melbourne, Australia. E-mail:˜matthew.tam@unimelb.edu.au
October 22, 2026
Abstract

The Perception-Adjusted Luce Model (PALM) introduced by Echenique et al. (2018) is a sequential choice model that can accommodate violations of regularity and choice overload, behaviors not captured by the utility-maximization framework. Flores et al. (2019) studied the assortment problem under the PALM and proved that, for the case of two levels, there is always an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level. They also conjectured that revenue-ordered by levels remain optimal for the general PALM with any number of levels. We resolve this question in the affirmative by showing that every PALM instance admits an optimal assortment that includes, within each level, all products at or above a level-specific revenue threshold. The proof involves first showing how the conjecture which deals with a discrete optimization problem, can be reduced to proving certain property of a related continuous optimization problem. Specifically, we study a continuous refinement of the assortment decision under the same PALM choice rule. Although the refinement permits partial utility selections, we prove it always has an optimum that selects complete revenue tiers. This allows us to show that the assortment problem is polynomial-time solvable when the number of levels is fixed.

Keywords: assortment optimization, revenue management, continuous optimization, revenue-ordered assortments.

1 Introduction

In the field of revenue management, the assortment problem consists of choosing what subset of products to show to customers in order to maximize the expected revenue. This problem has multiple applications in a diverse set of industries including airlines, retail, accommodation, and hospitality. The difficulty of solving a given assortment problem is typically dependent on the way customer behavior is modeled. For some consumer choice models such as the multinomial logit model (MNL), the random consideration set choice model or the Markov chain choice model, the corresponding assortment problem can be solved efficiently (Talluri and Van Ryzin, 2004; Gallego and Li, 2024; Blanchet et al., 2016). For other choice models such as the latent class multinomial logit (LC-MNL) model, the exponomial choice model or the ranked-list choice model, the assortment problem is NP-hard (Bront et al., 2009; Lu, 2026; Aouad et al., 2018).

Most assortment studies use a random utility framework in which consumers maximize utilities drawn from a menu-independent distribution. These models, known as random utility models (RUMs), satisfy a property called regularity (Block and Marschak, 1960): the probability of choosing an existing product cannot increase when another product is added to the offer set. However, substantial empirical evidence indicates that consumers often violate regularity and, consequently, that their behavior cannot always be explained by a RUM. One prominent example is the decoy effect or attraction effect, whereby adding an inferior alternative that is asymmetrically dominated by one of the existing products increases the probability that consumers choose the dominating product (Huber et al., 1982). A related phenomenon is the compromise effect: when a new product with extreme attribute values is introduced, an existing product may become the intermediate or “compromise” option and therefore more attractive (Simonson, 1989). In both cases, the addition of an option can increase the choice probability of an existing product, violating regularity. A further departure from standard rational-choice predictions is the paradox of choice or choice overload, where the increase of the number of available alternatives can increase the likelihood that consumers postpone the decision or make no purchase at all (Iyengar and Lepper, 2000; Long et al., 2025).

In the last 15 years, there has been an increased interest in studying consumer choice models that go beyond the RUM framework as a way to potentially explain and predict consumer choice behaviors such as the attraction effect and choice overload. One such model that has attracted considerable attention in the economics literature is the perception adjusted Luce model (PALM) proposed by Echenique et al. (2018). Under the PALM, consumers make choices via a finite sequential process following a perception priority order which permits violations of regularity and choice overload. Flores et al. (2019) considered the special case of the PALM where there are only two stages (or priorities) and proved that the assortment problem is polynomial time solvable. Specifically, the authors proved that there is always an optimal solution to the assortment problem that is revenue-ordered at each of the two stages (i.e. in each level if a product with revenue rr is offered, every product with revenue of at least rr is also offered). They also conjectured that the revenue-ordered by level structure is optimal for the general PALM (with any number of stages).

In this paper we resolve this conjecture: for every finite number of perception levels, assortment optimisation under PALM admits an optimal assortment that is revenue-ordered by level. Our proof considers a continuous refinement in which the firm may select part of each product’s utility while keeping revenues and perception levels fixed. Conditional on the total utility selected from each level, the best allocation selects utility in nonincreasing revenue order. The central step is to prove that the level totals can be jointly optimised at revenue-tier boundaries. At these boundaries, the refined decision selects complete tiers and therefore corresponds to an ordinary assortment. Enumerating the resulting level-specific thresholds gives a polynomial-time algorithm when the number of perception levels is fixed.

1.1 Related literature

To position our paper in the broader literature, we review some of the most related choice models and assortment optimization results. We begin with a review of results under choice models that, like PALM, are based on the MNL model but unlike the PALM, fall within the class of choice models based on random utility. We then proceed to review the main choice models and assortment optimization results for models, like the PALM, fall outside the RUM class.

Related results: RUM based choice models

The assortment optimization problem has already been studied for multiple choice models that are related to the PALM. One of the simplest heuristics to solve the assortment problem is to restrict the possible assortments to those that can be constructed as follows: choose a revenue threshold rr and then select all the products whose revenue is at least rr. The revenue-ordered assortment heuristic consists of evaluating the expected revenue of only those O⁡(n)O(n) assortments (where nn denotes the number of products) and return the assortment that yields the highest expected revenue. Although this heuristic is not guaranteed to produce an optimal solution, it has been shown that it is optimal for one of the most studied choice model known as the Luce or multinomial choice model (MNL) (Luce, 1965; Talluri and Van Ryzin, 2006).

There are many choice models that extend the MNL as the PALM. One extension considers that consumers are divided into k≥2k\geq 2 classes and each class behaves as a different MNL model. Under this model, known as the latent class MNL, revenue ordered assortments do not always yield an optimal solution to the assortment optimization problem. Moreover, it is shown that the problem is NP-hard (Bront et al., 2009; Rusmevichientong et al., 2014). Blanchet et al. (2016) proposed a Markov chain choice model which extends the MNL choice model and showed that the assortment optimization can be solved efficiently. However, Désir et al. (2020) proved the problem becomes NP-hard when the assortment is required to satisfy some maximum cardinality requirement. There has been a recent interest in the study of the assortment optimization problem for MNL based sequential choice models but unlike the PALM, they belong to the RUM class. Liu et al. (2020) studied the assortment problem for a sequential choice model that extends the MNL called the multinomial logit model under sequential offerings. Unlike the PALM in which the perception levels are fixed, their model allows the firm to optimize the stage at which consumers are allowed to observe each product. Another difference with the PALM is that their model cannot explain consumer behaviors that falls outside the RUM class such as choice overload or the attraction effect. The authors showed that the assortment problem is NP-hard. Later, Feldman and Segev (2022) showed the existence of a PTAS for the assortment problem under the same model. Gao et al. (2021) considers a similar RUM model as in Liu et al. (2020) in which the utility of the outside option; rather than being re-sampled at each stage, it is sampled once at the beginning of the process. The authors proved that the assortment problem can be solved in polynomial time. Wang et al. (2026) and Xu and Wang (2023) extend these sequential choice models by allowing customers to buy multiple products. In a related dynamic setting, Tang et al. (2023) study multi-period assortment optimization under an MNL model in which product attractiveness depends on cumulative past sales.

Related results: choice models outside the RUM framework

Tversky and Kahneman (1974) and Tversky and Kahneman (1981) provide some of the earliest empirical evidence that individuals sometimes violate regularity and therefore choice models based on the random utility maximization (RUM) framework may fail to explain choice behavior. Wernerfelt (1995) shows how consumers can use the composition of market offerings to infer product utilities, providing a rational explanation of the compromise effect. Kamenica (2008) considers a model in which the consumers are uninformed and can infer the value they get from an alternative depending on the complete offer set and showed that the model can explain RUM violations. The model we consider in this paper was introduced by Echenique et al. (2018) under the name of Perception Adjusted Luce Model (PALM). Under the PALM, each product has a predetermined perception level in the integer range [k]={1,2,…,k}[k]=\{1,2,\ldots,k\}. Consumer selection process occurs via a sequential mechanism and at each stage i∈[k]i\in[k], the consumer probability to choose an item of perception level ii follows the multinomial logit formula taking into account all the products that are available in all levels. The authors provide a clean characterization of what choice models can be explained by the PALM and show that the model can explain violations to regularity and choice overload. Flores et al. (2019) considers the sequential multinomial choice model (SMNL) in which products are divided into two categories and consumers follow the same sequential processes defined under the PALM. Under the SMNL, which is generalization of the MNL, Flores et al. (2019) proved that there is always an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level. The authors left the corresponding arbitrary-level statement for the PALM as an open conjecture.

Echenique and Saito (2019) and Ahumada and Ülkü (2018) have independently proposed a model known as the General Luce model (GLM) in which consumers discard some products using consideration sets as a filter prior to selecting an alternative based on the MNL formula. The GLM allows violations to regularity. Kleinberg et al. (2017) proposed a choice model where each consumer has a ranking of all products and chooses the ℓt​h\ell^{th} alternative from that ranking among those being offered. The authors prove that this model can incorporate violations of regularity as long as k>1k>1. Berbeglia and Venkataraman (2018) extends this model by considering a consumer is sampled from a probability distribution among all possible rankings and integer values for ℓ\ell. The authors show that the resulting model can have better predictions than RUM models in some real datasets.

1.2 Paper outline and proof strategy

To establish the conjecture posed by Flores et al. (2019), our proof strategy is as follows. In Section 2, we first consider a refined version of the assortment problem in which the utility of each product can be chosen continuously, rather than requiring products to be either fully included or excluded. Without loss of optimality, we show that products within each level can be selected in decreasing order of revenue. This observation allows us to reformulate the refined problem in terms of the total utility allocated to each level, substantially reducing its complexity. As a result, we show that the conjecture would hold if the refined problem has an optimal solution whose allocated total utility at each level ii matches the total utility of the αi\alpha_{i} products with highest revenue in level ii for some αi≥0\alpha_{i}\geq 0. In Section 3, we then exploit the structure of the resulting objective function of the refined problem. One of the key insights in the proof is that, for the refined problem, every positive-valued local maximizer with at least two non-zero coordinates is necessarily utility-integral. Finally, we provide some concluding remarks and some future research directions in Section 4.

2 Assortment Optimization under the Perception-Adjusted Luce Model

In this section, we formally introduce the Perception-Adjusted Luce Model (PALM), and formulate the traditional and refined assortment optimization under it. By analyzing the structure of the latter, we show that if an optimum of the refined assortment problem satisfies a property we call utility integral then there is an optimal solution to the traditional assortment optimization problem that is revenue-ordered-by-level.

2.1 Traditional assortment optimization under the PALM

The perception-adjusted Luce model (PALM), introduced by Echenique et al. (2018), considers a finite product set XX partitioned into ordered perception levels X1,…,XkX_{1},\ldots,X_{k}. Products in the same level have equal priority, and lower-indexed levels are considered first. This is equivalent to specifying a weak perception order. Each product gg has utility ug>0u_{g}>0 and revenue rg≥0r_{g}\geq 0. The outside option represents no purchase and has utility z≥0z\geq 0 and revenue zero.

For an assortment S⊆XS\subseteq X, let x=(x1,…,xk)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) denote its associated vector, where

xi=∑g∈S∩Xiug,x_{i}=\sum_{g\in S\cap X_{i}}u_{g}, (2.1)

and let

D⁡(z,x)=z+∑i=1kxi.D(z,x)=z+\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}. (2.2)

Thus xix_{i} is the sum of the utility of the products from level ii that belong to SS, and D⁡(z,x)D(z,x) consists of the sum of the utility of the products in SS plus the utility of the outside option.

Definition 2.1 (PALM).

Given an assortment S⊆XS\subseteq X, a consumer visits the levels in order. Conditional on reaching level ii, the consumer selects each product g∈S∩Xig\in S\cap X_{i} with probability ug/D⁡(z,x)u_{g}/D(z,x), and move to the next level without purchasing with probability 1−xi/D⁡(z,x)1-x_{i}/D(z,x). The unconditional probability of selecting product g∈Xig\in X_{i} is

𝒫⁡(g,S)=ugD⁡(z,x)​∏h<i(1−xhD⁡(z,x)),g∈S∩Xi.\mathcal{P}(g,S)=\frac{u_{g}}{D(z,x)}\prod_{h<i}\left(1-\frac{x_{h}}{D(z,x)}\right),\qquad g\in S\cap X_{i}. (2.3)

The probability of no purchase is ∏i=1k(1−xi/D⁡(z,x))\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-x_{i}/D(z,x)). For an empty assortment, no purchase occurs with probability one, including when z=0z=0.

The denominator in PALM includes the entire assortment and remains the same at every stage. With one nonempty level, PALM reduces to the Luce model; with several nonempty levels, no purchase can have positive probability even when z=0z=0. For D⁡(z,x)>0D(z,x)>0, the expected revenue obtained by offering the assortment SS whose associated vector is xx becomes

𝖱𝖾𝗏PALM​(S)=∑i=1k∑g∈S∩Xiug​rgD⁡(z,x)​∏h<i(1−xhD⁡(z,x)).\mathsf{Rev}^{\mathrm{PALM}}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\sum_{g\in S\cap X_{i}}u_{g}r_{g}}{D(z,x)}\prod_{h<i}\left(1-\frac{x_{h}}{D(z,x)}\right). (2.4)

The traditional assortment optimization problem (or assortment problem in short) consists of finding an assortment S⊆XS\subseteq X that maximizes 𝖱𝖾𝗏PALM​(S)\mathsf{Rev}^{\mathrm{PALM}}(S).

Definition 2.2 (Revenue-ordered by level).

An assortment S⊆XS\subseteq X is revenue-ordered by level if, for each level ii, the inclusion of a product g∈S∩Xig\in S\cap X_{i} in SS implies the inclusion of every product h∈Xih\in X_{i} with rh≥rgr_{h}\geq r_{g}. Equivalently, for each level ii, there is a threshold τi∈{rg:g∈Xi}∪{+∞}\tau_{i}\in\{r_{g}:g\in X_{i}\}\cup\{+\infty\} such that

S∩Xi={g∈Xi:rg≥τi}.S\cap X_{i}=\{g\in X_{i}:r_{g}\geq\tau_{i}\}.

Flores et al. (2019) proved the following result for the case of a PALM with two levels and left open the conjecture that follows.

Theorem 2.3 (Two-level SML (Flores et al., 2019)).

If k=2k=2, the assortment problem under PALM has an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level.

Conjecture 2.4 (Revenue-ordered by level for PALM (Flores et al., 2019)).

The assortment problem under PALM admits an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level.

A major obstacle to proving this conjecture is the interaction between assortment decisions across levels. Although the choice process is sequential, a product’s purchase probability depends on the assortments offered at its own level and at all preceding and following levels. Establishing the optimality of revenue ordering at every level therefore requires a careful analysis of these non-linear interactions and their effect on total revenue. We prove Conjecture 2.4 by studying a refined version of the assortment problem under the PALM which we introduce next.

2.2 Refined assortment optimization under the PALM

In the traditional assortment problem, each product is either offered in full or omitted. In the refined assortment problem under PALM, the firm may reduce the utility of any product gg to u~g∈[0,ug]\tilde{u}_{g}\in[0,u_{g}]. Berbeglia et al. (2021) studied the refined assortment optimization problem and showed that for several choice models the optimal refined assortment revenue is strictly higher than the traditional assortment revenue. To study the refined problem under the PALM, the revenues and perception levels remain the same and choice probabilities follow the same PALM rule with the selected utilities u~g\tilde{u}_{g}. Taking u~g∈{0,ug}\tilde{u}_{g}\in\{0,u_{g}\} for every product recovers every traditional assortment.

For a refined decision, let xi=∑g∈Xiu~gx_{i}=\sum_{g\in X_{i}}\tilde{u}_{g} denote the total selected utility at level ii and write

D⁡(z,x)=z+∑ixi.D(z,x)=z+\sum_{i}x_{i}.

A key observation about the refined model is that, for fixed level totals x1,…,xkx_{1},\dots,x_{k}, the expected revenue is maximized by allocating utility to products in decreasing order of revenue within each level. Indeed, transferring equal utility from a lower-revenue product to higher-revenue product within the same level increases the expected revenue from that level without changing the revenue obtained from the other levels.

This observation allows the optimal allocation within each level to be described using a single-function. For each level ii, let UiU_{i} denote the total available utility given by

Ui=∑g∈Xiug.U_{i}=\sum_{g\in X_{i}}u_{g}.

Arrange the products in XiX_{i} in nonincreasing revenue order and partition [0,Ui][0,U_{i}] into consecutive intervals, assigning each product gg an interval of length ugu_{g}. Define Pi:[0,Ui]→ℝ+P_{i}:[0,U_{i}]\to\mathbb{R}_{+} to equal rgr_{g} on the interval assigned to gg. Thus, PiP_{i} is a nonincreasing step function. Merging adjacent intervals with equal revenue gives its revenue tiers. The construction is illustrated in Figure 1.

The revenue at level ii obtainable from utility xi∈[0,Ui]x_{i}\in[0,U_{i}] is the area under this curve:

Ai​(xi)=∫0xiPi​(t)​𝑑t.A_{i}(x_{i})=\int_{0}^{x_{i}}P_{i}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. (2.5)

In other words, Ai​(xi)A_{i}(x_{i}) is obtained by allocating xix_{i} of utility to the highest-revenue product first. Furthermore, since PiP_{i} is a weakly decreasing step function, AiA_{i} is continuous, nondecreasing, piecewise linear and concave.

Let ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} denote the set of breakpoints of AiA_{i}, together with the endpoints 00 and UiU_{i}. In other words, these are points where PiP_{i} drops to a strictly lower revenue. We call xi∈[0,Ui]x_{i}\in[0,U_{i}] utility-integral if xi∈ℬix_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{i}. Figure 1 illustrates the construction.

For a given xx with D⁡(z,x)>0D(z,x)>0, the best refined revenue at these level totals is

𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,x)=∑i=1kAi​(xi)D⁡(z,x)​∏h<i(1−xhD⁡(z,x)).\mathsf{Rev}(z,x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{A_{i}(x_{i})}{D(z,x)}\prod_{h<i}\left(1-\frac{x_{h}}{D(z,x)}\right). (2.6)

This is the traditional assortment revenue formula (2.4), except that each numerator is replaced by its best fractional value Ai​(xi)A_{i}(x_{i}). Every xi∈[0,Ui]x_{i}\in[0,U_{i}] is attainable by a partial selection, so the refined assortment problem is

max0≤xi≤Ui​(i=1,…,k)⁡𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,x).\max_{0\leq x_{i}\leq U_{i}\ (i=1,\ldots,k)}\mathsf{Rev}(z,x). (2.7)

The all-zero selection has revenue zero, including when z=0z=0.

Next, we relate utility integrality in the refined assortment problem to revenue ordering in the traditional assortment problem.

2.3 From refined integrality to revenue-ordered assortments

The following proposition turns a utility-integral optimum of the refined assortment problem (i.e. xi∗∈ℬix^{*}_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{i} for all ii) into a revenue-ordered optimum of the traditional assortment problem.

Proposition 2.5 (Existence of a revenue-ordered-by-level optimum).

If the refined problem has an optimum with xi∗∈ℬix^{*}_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{i} for every level, then the traditional assortment problem under the PALM has a revenue-ordered-by-level optimum with the same revenue.

Proof.

For any ordinary assortment SS, take xi=∑g∈S∩Xiugx_{i}=\sum_{g\in S\cap X_{i}}u_{g}. Since Ai​(xi)A_{i}(x_{i}) is the largest numerator obtainable at this utility,

∑g∈S∩Xiug​rg≤Ai​(xi).\sum_{g\in S\cap X_{i}}u_{g}r_{g}\leq A_{i}(x_{i}).

All coefficients multiplying these numerators in (2.4) are nonnegative. Hence 𝖱𝖾𝗏PALM​(S)≤𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,x)\mathsf{Rev}^{\mathrm{PALM}}(S)\leq\mathsf{Rev}(z,x), so the refined optimum is an upper bound on every ordinary assortment’s revenue.

Now let x∗x^{*} be a utility-integral refined optimum. In each level, select complete tiers in decreasing revenue order until their cumulative utility is xi∗x_{i}^{*}, and let S∗S^{*} be the resulting assortment. Its level utilities are xi∗x_{i}^{*} and its level numerators are exactly Ai​(xi∗)A_{i}(x_{i}^{*}). Consequently,

𝖱𝖾𝗏PALM​(S∗)=𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,x∗).\mathsf{Rev}^{\mathrm{PALM}}(S^{*})=\mathsf{Rev}(z,x^{*}). (2.8)

Thus S∗S^{*} attains the refined upper bound and is optimal among all ordinary assortments. The same conclusion holds for the empty selection by the zero-revenue convention. ∎

In light of proposition (2.5), one way to prove the Conjecture (2.4) is to show that the refined assortment problem has an optimal solution that is utility-integral. We show this in the next section.

3 Utility-Integrality in the Refined Problem

Our main theorem establishes utility integrality for the refined assortment problem under PALM.

Theorem 3.1 (Utility-integrality of refined problem).

Let k≥1k\geq 1 and z≥0z\geq 0. Then the refined problem (2.7) has an optimal solution x∗x^{*} that is utility-integral. In other words, x∗=(x1∗,…,xk∗)x^{*}=(x^{*}_{1},\dots,x_{k}^{*}) with xi∗∈ℬix_{i}^{*}\in\mathcal{B}_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k.

Another consequence of Theorem 3.1 is that under the PALM, the refined assortment optimization yields exactly the same revenue as the traditional assortment optimization. This extends a result of Berbeglia et al. (2021) who showed that both problems yield the same revenue under the MNL choice model (a special case of the PALM with k=1k=1 levels).

The remainder of this section is concerned with the proof of Theorem 3.1. The main difficulty in the analysis arises in the case when z>0z>0 and k≥2k\geq 2. In Subsection 3.1, we establish a key intermediate result: if z>0z>0 and k≥2k\geq 2, then every local maximizer of 𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,⋅)\mathsf{Rev}(z,\cdot) with positive objective value and at least two non-zero coordinates is necessarily utility-integral. The proof of this result follows by combining first-order optimality conditions with a curvature argument that rules out utility-fractional coordinates. In Subsection 3.2, we use this result to establish Theorem 3.1, treating the limit cases where z=0z=0 or at most one coordinate is non-zero separately.

Given a feasible point x=(x1,…,xk)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) for the refined assortment problem, we say level ii of xx is active if xi>0x_{i}>0 and inactive if xi=0x_{i}=0.

Proposition 3.5.

Let z>0z>0 and x≥0x\geq 0. Suppose xx is local maximizer of 𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,⋅)\mathsf{Rev}(z,\cdot) with at least two active levels and 𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,x)>0\mathsf{Rev}(z,x)>0. Then xx is utility-integral.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we delete inactive levels and relabel the remaining levels without changing their order. Note that this preserves local optimality. Since there are at least two active levels, we may therefore assume that x>0x>0 and k≥2k\geq 2.

Suppose that xjx_{j} is a fractional coordinate. Since xjx_{j} lies in the interior of its current revenue tier, the first-order optimality yields 𝖱𝖾𝗏xj=0\mathsf{Rev}_{x_{j}}=0. By Lemma 3.3, we have 𝖱𝖾𝗏z<0\mathsf{Rev}_{z}<0 and so Lemma 3.4 implies 𝖱𝖾𝗏xj​xj>0\mathsf{Rev}_{x_{j}x_{j}}>0. This contradicts the second-order necessary condition 𝖱𝖾𝗏xj​xj≤0\mathsf{Rev}_{x_{j}x_{j}}\leq 0 for a local maximum at an interior point. We therefore conclude that xx has no fractional coordinates. ∎

3.2 Proof of Theorem 3.1

We are finally ready to present the proof of our main theorem.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

First suppose z=0z=0. If the zero vector is an optimal solution, then there is nothing to prove, so suppose all optima are non-zero. Let

pmax:=max{Pi(t):t∈[0,Ui],i=1,…,k}p_{\max}:=\max\{P_{i}(t):t\in[0,U_{i}],\,i=1,\dots,k\}

be the largest value of any revenue tier so that Ai​(xi)≤pmax​xiA_{i}(x_{i})\leq p_{\max}x_{i} for all i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k. For x≠0x\neq 0, we have D=∑i=1kxi>0D=\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}>0 and qi=xiDq_{i}=\frac{x_{i}}{D}, and so ∑ici​qi=1−∏i(1−xiD)≤1\sum_{i}c_{i}q_{i}=1-\prod_{i}\left(1-\frac{x_{i}}{D}\right)\leq 1. Consequently, we obtain the upper bound

𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(0,x)=∑i=1kAi​(xi)D​ci≤pmax​∑i=1kqi​ci≤pmax.\mathsf{Rev}(0,x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{A_{i}(x_{i})}{D}c_{i}\leq p_{\max}\sum_{i=1}^{k}q_{i}c_{i}\leq p_{\max}. (3.17)

Let i∗∈{1,…,k}i^{*}\in\{1,\dots,k\} be a level whose first tier has value pmaxp_{\max}, and let bi∗b_{i^{*}} be the endpoint of the tier. That is, Pi∗​(t)=pmaxP_{i^{*}}(t)=p_{\max} for t∈[0,bi∗]t\in[0,b_{i^{*}}]. Then setting x∗=bi∗​ei∗x^{*}=b_{i^{*}}{e_{i^{*}}} gives

𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(0,x∗)=Ai∗​(bi∗)bi∗=pmax.\mathsf{Rev}(0,x^{*})=\frac{A_{i^{*}}(b_{i^{*}})}{b_{i^{*}}}=p_{\max}.

In other words, x∗x^{*} is a feasible point that attains the upper bound (3.17) with xi∗∈ℬix^{*}_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k. Thus x∗x^{*} is an optimal solution of the refined problem which is utility-integral.

Now suppose z>0z>0. Then the function 𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,⋅)\mathsf{Rev}(z,\cdot) is continuous on the set of nonnegative vectors. Since the feasible region of refined assortment problem (2.7) is the product of closed intervals, it is a compact set. Hence existence of a global optimum x∗x^{*} follows by the Extreme Value Theorem. If no coordinate of x∗x^{*} is fractional, there is nothing to prove, so suppose there is at least one. Without loss of generality, we can delete all inactive levels and relabel the remaining active levels without changing their order. Since an inactive level has Ai​(0)=0A_{i}(0)=0 and survival factor one, this leaves the objective unchanged and preserves global optimality. Let mm denote the number of active levels.

If the optimal value is zero, then the all-zero vector is a utility-integral optimum. Hence we need only consider the case where the optimal value is positive. If m≥2m\geq 2, then Proposition 3.5 contradicts the existence of a fractional coordinate of x∗x^{*}, so it remains only to consider case with m=1m=1. Inside any constant-revenue tier, we have A1​(x)=a+p​xA_{1}(x)=a+px for some a,p∈ℝa,p\in\mathbb{R}. Thus 𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,x)=a+p​xz+x\mathsf{Rev}(z,x)=\frac{a+px}{z+x} and so

dd​x​𝖱𝖾𝗏​(z,x)=p​z−a(z+x)2.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\mathsf{Rev}(z,x)=\frac{pz-a}{(z+x)^{2}}.

Since the sign of this derivative is constant throughout the tier, 𝖱𝖾𝗏⁡(z,⋅)\mathsf{Rev}(z,\cdot) is either monotone or constant on that tier. In either case, if an interior point of the tier is optimal, then one of its endpoints is also optimal.

Thus in every case there exists a global optimum x∗x^{*} with xi∗∈ℬix_{i}^{*}\in\mathcal{B}_{i} for all i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k. This completes the proof. ∎

4 Concluding remarks and future research

We studied assortment optimization, a central problem in revenue management, under the perception-adjusted Luce model (PALM) of Echenique et al. (2018). PALM is an early sequential extension of the Luce model that accommodates violations of regularity and choice overload. We proved that there exists an optimal assortment that is revenue-ordered by level: within each level, all products at or above a level-specific revenue threshold are offered. This resolves the conjecture of Flores et al. (2019) and extends their two-level result to the general PALM. Our result reduces the assortment decision to the choice of one threshold per level and yields a polynomial-time algorithm when the number of levels is fixed.

Methodologically, we established this discrete structural result using continuous optimization techniques. Our technique is a substantial departure from the algebraic proof by Flores et al. (2019) for k=2k=2. We considered the refined assortment problem in which the firm may reduce the utilities of the products being offered. We then used utility-preserving exchanges and first- and second-order optimality conditions to show that the refined assortment problem has an optimum that corresponds to an ordinary assortment, so the two problems have the same optimal revenue.

We provide two research directions worthy of further study. Operational restrictions such as cardinality and shelf-space constraints are common in many businesses. These constraints may prevent the inclusion of all products above a revenue threshold and may invalidate the use of optimality conditions used in our proof. Characterizing the structure of optimal constrained assortments, and developing algorithms with approximation guarantees where exact optimization is difficult would be interesting. Finally, the exactness of the continuous refinement raises a methodological question beyond PALM. Our proof uses the common utility denominator and the ordered sequence of perception levels. Identifying conditions under which a similar argument applies to other sequential choice models, or to restricted forms of customer heterogeneity, would provide a clearer picture about the scope of our approach. When the refinement is no longer exact, quantifying the gap between refined and traditional assortment revenues could help assess its usefulness for constructing bounds and approximation algorithms.
